Testimony of Dr. Alexander P. Mayer, Yarmouth, ME
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgeon, MaineGenera| April 28, 2025
Good afternoon, my name is Alexander Mayer. I'm a reconstructive surgeon at Maine General. I am a native New Englander and did my undergrad at Colby College. I subsequently went away to do my medical training and fellowship and finally returned to
Maine to practice. I happen to be the only reconstructive surgeon in our health system.
When I started at Maine General in 2022, I was told to anticipate a waiting period of 5 to 9 months for my enrollment into MaineCare. During that time it proved very difficult to
see and treat patients with MaineCare at all. This unfortunately represents a huge
portion of our patient population.
Many of the medically necessary procedures that these patients were seeking needed prior authorization. However, during the provider enrollment period, there was no way to
verify if these MaineCare patients met the criteria for prior authorization. We were
placed into the position of either deferring care for these patients until the enrollment
was complete, or providing care to these patients with the hope that they would ultimately meet the criteria for surgery and the hospital would get reimbursed. Unfortunately, this did lead to situations where patients did not meet the MaineCare criteria and the hospital was refused appropriate reimbursement for procedures.
Beyond procedures, prescription medications and testing posed similar issues. Prescriptions requiring prior authorization would be kicked back from the pharmacy but I had no recourse to submit the prior authorization since I was not yet fully enrolled.
All of this is to say, patients were kept from getting procedures in a timely manner, kept from getting medications for their ongoing treatment and recovery, and experienced
significant limitations in their access to care. This was due to the prolonged enrollment
period and inability to verify prior authorization criteria during that time.
Ultimately, it took nearly 5 months for my enrollment to be complete and during that time I had the opportunity to discuss with other members of our hospital, including hospital
administration, primary care physicians, and other surgeons, whether they had
experienced similar issues in the past. I was shocked to discover widespread frustration with these issues at all levels of our institution. It was at this point that I began discussions with Rep. Arford to see how we might improve access to care for these
patients. I am hopeful that LD 1758 can help accelerate provider enrollment to
MaineCare, while expanding patient's timely access to care.

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services
Committee, my name is Jeffrey Austin and I am presenting testimony in support of LD 1758 on
behalf of the Maine Hospital Association. Our colleagues at the Maine Medical Association and

the Maine Osteopathic Association are signing-on to this testimony as well.
Purpose. The purpose of this legislation to increase the efficiency of an administrative process for hospitals and potentially other providers. Increasing administrative efficiency is a constant effort for our members and its an expectation of the public. There will always be administrative
tasks, but we all have a responsibility to ensure that the tasks can be completed as efficiently as possible. Currently, the administrative task associated with MaineCare about which we hear the
'
most frustration is the provider enrollment process.
To be clear, this is not a reflection of the DHHS individuals who oversee the process. We
consistently hear that they try and work with hospitals and offer as much flexibility as possible.
The challenge, as we understand it, is rooted in the software system that is used for enrollment.
The "real" solution to the problem would be to replace the platform. Any legislation seeking to
do that would have a fiscal note and would assuredly be unsuccessful.
This legislation is an attempt to improve the process using the current platform.
Background. This legislation seeks to address the process providers must use to enroll providers
to treat MaineCare patients. From our perspective it's called "enrollment"; from the DHHS
perspective it's called "credentialling." I will call it enrollment in this testimony.
Before a provider may work for a hospital, the hospital reviews the qualifications of the individual.
That is our credentialling process and it is quite extensive.
1

Once the hospital has credentialled the provider, we must enroll the provider with each payer:
Medicare, Medicaid and commercial payers.
Obviously, payers like MaineCare should review the qualifications of providers (credential them)
before they agree to reimburse for their services.
But, there are unnecessary hurdles due to the process as it stands today.
"Batch" cases. When a hospital submits an application to enroll a provider, it is called a "case." At the hospital's discretion, we may include more than one provider in a case. For large hospitals, its not uncommon to have more than 100 individual providers in the case.
There are two limitations with the current DHHS batch case process.
The first is that all providers in the case must be approved before the system can enroll any
of them. So, if 99 out of 100 cases are approved, they can't be enrolled until the l00`h is also
approved. The platform is so complex that it is simply unlikely that We will be able to submit a
case of 100+ providers that has no flaws. So, if there is one case with challenges, the entire batch
is delayed.
You will hear from DHHS that if hospitals would only limit their case size their cases would be
processed more quickly. Undoubtedly, that is true. Small cases with l-2 providers are approved
relatively quickly.
The reason we don't though, is the second problem with the current DHHS batch process is that each hospital may only have one case open at a time. That is apparently a limitation of the platform. Although we're not 100% sure of that. It may be an operational policy. We would be happy to send 50 cases with l-2 providers per case. But we can't. We can only send l case at a
time.
A complicating wrinkle is one of the DHHS flexibilities that we really appreciate. Once a case is
open, but before the providers have been formally enrolled, we can put the provider to work on
the floor and have them see Medicaid patients. The reason is that DHHS will reimburse us for
the Work done by the provider retroactively to the date the case was opened (as long as the provider was ultimately enrolled).
So, we have an incentive to load as many providers into one case.
Picture 100 doctors standing on a platfonn waiting for a train. Each train is a case that has to leave
the hospital, go to DHHS, and return` . If the train has only 5 provides on it, it will return quickly.
However, the other 95 doctors can not be put to work. It will take Weeks and weeks to get through

If the doctors can work in the meantime, who cares?
The reason we care is during the 6-months that it takes DHHS to process the 100-provider case, another 100 providers pile-up on the platform. Those providers can NOT see Medicaid patients.
If we could send a second case, we could allow them to see Medicaid patients. But, the system

Other Problems. There are other aspects of the current system that seem unnecessarily
bureaucratic to us. We think MaineCare requires a full enrollment review in too many situations that are not necessary. We aren't sure if these are policy requirements or functional requirements
due to the system they use.

For example, providers who have gone through the enrollment process and have been in good
standing for 10 years have to re-enroll if they change the location of their practice.
Commercial carriers, for example, don't require re-enrollment. We simply notify them of a
'
provider's address change. Not so MaineCare, it requires re-enrollment.
Another example is the requirement to enroll the "NOPRs." These are staff that are: _l\lon-billing,
Qrdering, Brescribing, and Referring providers. These are private practice physicians. They are independently enrolled in MaineCare. However, sometimes their patients access our facilities (for a lab or x-ray). The hospital is enrolled in MaineCare, the independent doctor is enrolled in MaineCare, but the hospital has not enrolled the doctor as a hospital provider (because he/she is
not). Yet, we still have to enroll them. Medicare does not require this. We don't know if this is
MaineCare policy or a requirement due to the limitations of MaineCare's current platform.

The Legislation. As we said earlier, the best solution would be to change the platform.
would result in a fiscal note.

That

So, we have proposed this solution, which does not appear to have any need for a fiscal note to us.
It requires DHHS to essentially approve the case/application upon receipt -- provisionally.
Our vision is that this method would allow DHHS to do two things. First, they could immediately
retum the case without doing the actual verification work for each individual provider. Then We
could send another case and so-on. Second, DHHS could take up to 60 days to do any in-depth
verification for each provider that has been provisionally approved. We're not suggesting they
shouldn't review the providers if they want to. But, it would allow us to keep filing more cases while they do their reviews.

Obviously, we need DHHS staff to continue their current practice (greatly appreciated) of working with us when a document is missing or there is some technical shortcoming in the application. We
would be frustrated if they changed their existing protocol in response to this legislation.
We've set some pre-requisites in the legislation that must be met in order to take advantage of this provisional approval model. We're open to discussing those pre-requisites.

Conclusion. I want to reiterate our appreciation for the staff at DHHS and their willingness to help make the current system work better. We believe that what We are looking for could not be
done by staff Without some legislative approval.
On behalf of hospitals, I take a lot of criticism for the administrative expenses at hospitals and in
healthcare generally. They are not all accurate; but they are not all unfounded either.

Much of what hospitals do in the realm of `administration' is try and navigate systems established
by others - payers and the government. We can't reduce administrative expenses unilaterally. We

need your help.

LD 1758 An Act to Expedite Provider Enrollment in MaineCare
Testimony in Support April 28, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my name is Karen Hawkes, and I am speaking today on behalf of Northern Light Health and our member organizations in support of this bill. I am the Vice President of Population Health for Northern Light Health, and I have senior level responsibility for provider credentialing with our payers.
I first want to express my deep appreciation for the staff and leadership of the Department of Health & Human Services and more specifically, the Office of MaineCare Services. Members of the provider enrollment team at MaineCare have been extremely receptive to our feedback over the years and assist us as much as possible to move enrollment cases to completion. My testimony today is in no way a reflection of their work or efforts.
To help you understand why this bill is needed I want to begin my testimony describing the challenges with MaineCare credentialling, all of which are centered around the credentialling platform. Unlike other payers, which offer a rather straight forward application process or allow for roster submission that is initiated prior to a provider's onboarding, the MaineCare platform restricts the enrollment process to a single case at a time. For our hospitals, a single case consists of multiple provider and facility enrollment requests and changes. For example, just yesterday we submitted a new case for Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center that included 118 new provider enrollment requests and 22 enrollment changes. Given the size of this case, we are anticipating it could take up to 6 months for this case to close. It is not until this case closes that our enrollment team is able to initiate a new case, start the cumbersome data entry process, and submit a new case for payer credentialing. Currently, EMMC is holding $20M in MaineCare claims for services rendered by providers pending MaineCare enrollment.
In addition to the single case restriction, there are nuances to the platform and MaineCare's credentialing process that are highly unique and labor intensive. For example, only one user may be in a case at one time prohibiting a team approach. When preparing a new case, the user must review previously entered data from the prior case and confirm accuracy before a new case can be successfully submitted. Given the depth of data review and scope of data entry, it is expected that there will be several requests for additional information that may have been missed or perhaps expired at the time the case was open. While we appreciate the opportunity to respond to these requests for information to ensure the case progresses, it does extend the timeline toward enrollment.

The challenges are significant and for our largest hospital our providers wait a year for MaineCare to complete the credentialing process and approve them as a MaineCare provider. While difficult, there is an aspect of the current process that we need to retain should this bill move forward - an opportunity to respond to requests for more information and make corrections before a determination on case status is made.
This bill is a creative solution that allows the MaineCare credentialling structure to continue while creating a process that will address our primary concern, the time it takes for a provider to bill MaineCare for services. Under the bill, the Department of Health and Human Services must provisionally approve the enrollment application of a provider in good standing that has a national provider identifier within 48 hours of receipt of a complete application if the provider is employed by a health care entity that has an enrollment application approval rate of greater than 90% in the previous 5 years. The department may conduct a complete review during a 60-day expedited provisional approval period, but the provider is considered approved after 60 days if the department does not affirmatively deny approval during that period. There are protections for the department in the bill in that the bill does not prevent the department from suspending or revoking approval if a material deficiency exists.
Ultimately the credentialling system for MaineCare needs to be replaced with a structure that results in an expedited process for approval. I would encourage the exploration of delegated credentialing for Maine's larger health systems, reducing cost to the state and expediting enrollment. As you consider what the right long-term solution is, I do believe this bill is an important next step that allows the department the time it will take to restructure the credentialling process.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important legislation.

Senator Ingwersen, Chair Representative Meyer, Chair Members, Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0100
Re: LD 1758 - An Act to Expedite Provider Enrollment in MaineCare
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition to LD 1758 - An Act to Expedite Provider Enrollment in MaineCare.
This bill intends to establish an expedited process for providers to enroll in the MaineCare program. Under the bill, the Department of Health and Human Services (the "Department") must provisionally approve the enrollment application of a provider in good standing that has a national provider identifier within 48 hours of receipt of a complete application if the provider is employed by a health care entity that has an enrollment application approval rate of greater than 90% in the previous 5 years. The Department may conduct a complete review during a 60-day expedited provisional approval period, but the provider is considered approved after 60 days if the Department does not affirmatively deny approval during that period. However, the bill does not prevent the Department from suspending or revoking approval after the 60-day period if a material deficiency exists. If the provider's approval is revoked, the provider is not eligible for expedited reenrollment but must go through the regular enrollment process as established by rule. The Office of MaineCare Services may seek reimbursements for any payment made to a provider during the provisional period if the provider's provisional approval is revoked. The Department must adopt rules to implement these provisions.
This bill would violate and is preempted by federal law (42 CFR � 455.450(a)(1)) which expressly requires the state Medicaid Agency to "verify that a provider meets any applicable Federal regulations, or State requirements for the provider type prior to making an enrollment determination." The chances of improper payments or even fraud, waste, or abuse in the MaineCare program would increase as a result of the expedited process proposed by this bill. In addition, this bill imposes timelines on the Medicaid program that are vastly shorter than the credentialing timelines imposed by the state on commercial insurers (see 24 MRS � 4303(2)).
Passage of LD 1758 would result in increased work during the provider enrollment credentialing process for both the State and the State's credentialing vendor. Enrollment case denials would likely increase based on the arbitrary deadlines established by the bill and the inability to fully validate necessary information as short timelines do not allow for the procurement of all necessary information. The process would also result in additional work for the Department to identify and recoup improper payments made to providers whose provisional approval is subsequently revoked.
MaineCare's current systems architecture does not support the functionality proposed in LD 1758. This bill would require the Department to implement a substantial, lengthy, and costly system upgrade to meet the 48hour requirement. The Department has a planned system upgrade underway that is expected to conclude in October 2026; any system upgrade necessitated by this bill would have to wait until the current upgrade is

completed. A proposal from the Department's fiscal agent estimates a system change to allow us to review and make full determinations on enrollment applications within 48 hours would cost $7-8 million; the Department could request a 90% funding match from CMS for this implementation. However, this system change would not address the other requirements in this bill. The exact cost to meet the other requirements proposed in LD 1758 is unknown, but the Department estimates it would amount to hundreds of thousands of general fund dollars with potentially no federal match available because of the violation of federal law noted above. This infraction would also jeopardize existing federal match (75%) for ongoing provider enrollment operations.
The Department has made significant successful efforts over the past 12 to 18 months to reduce the turnaround time for enrollment cases. The average turnaround time to process an enrollment case in March 2025 was only 20 calendar days, down significantly from the November 2023 average of 64 days. The Department and its credentialing vendor have implemented several process improvements and continue to identify and implement efficiencies to automate or streamline functions to reduce both the number and size of provider enrollment cases. Examples include automatic updating of individual enrolled providers' licenses and of provider clinical laboratory improvement amendments - both of which used to require the provider to submit a case to update. Future enhancements include the automatic updating of facility licenses.
Finally, the timelines set forth in this LD would limit the ability of a provider to fix errors in enrollment cases and drive an increase in enrollment denials. This would require providers to re-enter and resubmit information a second time, increasing the administrative burden for providers and negatively affecting a provider's desired billing start date. In addition, providers would be unexpectedly financially impacted by reversed or recouped claims and may not have all the information necessary to make decisions about whether and when to start providing healthcare services MaineCare members.
The Department maintains that its efforts to reduce both the number and size of provider enrollment cases are the appropriate method for bringing down processing time while also meeting the Department's federal and state enrollment obligations. We would be happy to provide additional information and further discuss the challenges associated with LD 1758 and our opposition to moving forward with the bill. Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation.
Sincerely,
Michelle Probert Director Office of MaineCare Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services

The Problem
LD 1758 addresses a longstanding challenge with the MaineCare provider enrollment process;
that of providers waiting months to have their enrollment application approved. During this time, the provider cannot bill the MaineCare program for covered services so must wait for
payment on the back end, after their approval is secured. I am also concerned about the unintended yet potentially negative impact the current enrollment process may have on
MaineCare patients. Not only might their provider wait months to be approved and receive
payment for services delivered to them - medically necessary treatments and medications may
also be denied if they require prior authorization.
The primary source of this challenge is the MaineCare credentialling platform and the resulting slow and burdensome process for providers seeking enrollment in the MaineCare program. As
creating a new system would be prohibitively expensive, I am not proposing this.
The Solution
Rather, what this bill does is create a framework for significant improvement in the enrollment process by using the credentialling platform that is in place and establishing an expedited

application during the following sixty day period. Nothing in this bill prevents the department from suspending or revoking the provisional approval of an applicant following a complete review of their enrollment application. The bill also directs the department to adopt rules to implement the expedited approval process, providing an opportunity for providers to engage in
the detail of the rule with public comment and recommendations. This framework balances MaineCare providers need for timely approval of their enrollment applications, With the Departments responsibility to ensure applicants meet all the enrollment
requirements.
